title: Producing the first New Orleans jazz concert in Philadelphia
summary: Asked by the Newspaper Guild, Rose booked Jack Teagarden's new band with Sterling Bose and Fazola, plus Sidney Bechet, Sidney De Paris and Freddie Moore. Bechet taught him to send tickets as commitment.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: But even among these people, there was a consciousness of the personalities and the people that had recorded the early jazz. Some of those people, of course, were playing in swing bands. And the fact that I had this collection became very well known in school, and people used to come to my room all the time to listen to records. And to discuss with me the music that they were playing, and they were much interested in this. Well, in 1935, the American Newspaper Guild was about to, was planning an annual affair. They have a, like a, a ball, you see. And a young man who was then the radio editor of the Philadelphia Evening Bulletin, whose name was Park Breck, got the idea that it would be a good thing to have a New Orleans jazz concert. And he knew somebody who knew me. So they came to me and asked me if I knew of any way that it would be possible to put together a concert of authentic New Orleans jazz in Philadelphia. And the question then was, from my standpoint, who was in the neighborhood? And the, the guild was prepared to foot the bill for it. So, uh, after discussion, uh, since they were going to have a dance anyway, in addition to this, and these were to take place on different floors of the building, with a dance on the third floor and a jazz concert on the second floor, I proposed that the newly organized band of Jack Teagarden would be, uh, attractive to, to bring in. It was a band that didn't last very long, but it was fortunate enough to have, uh, people like Sterling Bose and Irving Fazola in the band. And then, uh, because of various grapevine considerations, I, I learned who was in New York among the musicians. And I got hold of Sidney Bechet and Sidney D. Paris and Freddie Moore, the drummer known as Gate Mouth Moore.
Now, had you done any of this kind of thing before?
Well, how, how did, how did it occur to you that you could get a hold of Sidney Bechet, for instance?
Well, I knew he was in New York.
Okay. But, I mean, you, you never were before, uh, in the role of doing this kind of thing, talking to musicians.
No, this was, this was my first experience with dealing with him. How about in New Orleans?
And you, you never had that kind of relationship with the musicians here, promoting their music?
No, there was nothing to promote. I mean, you, there was no, uh, uh, see, there was no such thing as a concept of a jazz concert.

It didn't exist. Okay. So, I called, uh, I called Bechet and I, and he suggested Sidney D. Paris and, and Gate Mouth. And, uh, so I just made a deal with him to bring him in. And, in fact, it was Sidney who taught me the procedure. He says, well, you send us the tickets. Uh, and as soon as we get the tickets, we'll consider that a firm commitment and we'll come in, you see. So, we set the time and, uh, I got some local musicians that I already knew from Philadelphia. And so, uh, everything came together. And in 1936, in the beginning of 1936, we had, uh, the jazz concert where tickets were sold for people to come in and sit down and listen to music. And, uh, uh, uh, then I invited musicians from the dance band upstairs to come down to participate. And so, we did have Jack T. Garden and Bose and Fazola. And, uh, the combination of all these musicians made, uh, really an excellent concert.
